p.src:
Electrostatic forces require no new mechanics. If $U(\mathbf x)$ is a potential energy, then $\mathbf F=-\nabla U(\mathbf x),$ and the usual argument gives conservation of kinetic plus potential energy. For a particle of charge $e$ in an electrostatic potential $V(\mathbf x)$, $U(\mathbf x)=eV(\mathbf x),
  \qquad
  \mathbf F_{\mathrm{el}}=-e\nabla V.$ Magnetic forces have a different form. They depend on the particle’s velocity, so they cannot be introduced merely by adding another ordinary potential energy. Nevertheless, they do follow from an action principle and admit both Lagrangian and Hamiltonian descriptions. Reaching that description requires a short but essential interlude in vector calculus.

p.src: The operational point of a field is locality. Imagine that a certain region is hidden inside a bag. To measure the electric field in that region, put a small test charge there and observe its acceleration. The force is determined by the field where the charge is located, not by a separate consultation with every distant source. The same statement applies to a magnetic field and a moving test charge. Later, the vector potential will force us to qualify this simple picture, but it is the right place to begin.

p.src:
For two vectors $\mathbf V$ and $\mathbf A$, one component of the cross product is $(\mathbf V\times\mathbf A)_x
  =
  V_yA_z-V_zA_y.$ The other two follow by cycling $x\to y\to z\to x$. It is useful to replace $x,y,z$ by the indices $1,2,3$. The Kronecker symbol is $\delta_{ij}
  =
  \begin{cases}
    1,&i=j,\\
    0,&i\ne j,
  \end{cases}$ and the Levi–Civita symbol is defined by $\epsilon_{123}=\epsilon_{231}=\epsilon_{312}=1,
  \qquad
  \epsilon_{132}=\epsilon_{321}=\epsilon_{213}=-1,$ with $\epsilon_{ijk}=0$ whenever any two indices coincide. A cyclic ordering around a three-hour clock gives the plus signs; reversing the direction gives the minus signs. Interchanging any pair of indices reverses the sign, so $\epsilon_{ijk}$ is completely antisymmetric.

p.src:
Replacing $\mathbf V$ by $\nabla$ defines the curl: $(\nabla\times\mathbf A)_i
  =
  \epsilon_{ijk}\frac{\partial A_k}{\partial x_j}.$ In ordinary components, $\begin{aligned}(\nabla\times\mathbf A)_x
  &=
  \frac{\partial A_z}{\partial y}
  -\frac{\partial A_y}{\partial z},\\
  (\nabla\times\mathbf A)_y
  &=
  \frac{\partial A_x}{\partial z}
  -\frac{\partial A_z}{\partial x},\\
  (\nabla\times\mathbf A)_z
  &=
  \frac{\partial A_y}{\partial x}
  -\frac{\partial A_x}{\partial y}.\end{aligned}$ Where divergence measures local spreading, curl measures local circulation. A fluid rotating around an axis has nonzero curl along that axis. The picture is particularly vivid for velocity fields, though the definition applies to any vector field.

p.src:
We have seen a velocity crossed with a fixed vector before. In a frame rotating with angular velocity $\boldsymbol\omega$, the Coriolis force can be written $\mathbf F_{\mathrm{Cor}}
  =
  2m\,\mathbf v\times\boldsymbol\omega.$ It has the same algebraic form as the magnetic force: $2m\boldsymbol\omega
  \quad\longleftrightarrow\quad
  \frac{e}{c}\mathbf B.$ A uniform magnetic field perpendicular to a plane therefore bends charged-particle trajectories in much the same way that a rotating frame deflects moving bodies.
